Relevant OSI discussion: http://lists.opensource.org/pipermail/license-review_lists.opensource.org/2023-August/005404.html

One slight comment on Unicode 3 (full disclosure: I helped draft it and have submitted it to OSI for approval; it is still in the OSI discussion loop as part of the approval process).
The canonical version (which I think is the version SPDX should be using here) uses the generic attribution notice:

Copyright © <YEAR(S)> <COPYRIGHT HOLDER>

The version you have linked to is the one that Unicode is using for its own code, in which they have inserted their own copyright notice:

Copyright © 1991-2023 Unicode, Inc.

So I’d suggest using the former, rather than the latter, for SPDX.

For anyone wanting to review that license (don’t think I can as it’s a bit of a conflict), I circulated on the mailing list a redlined version of the new v3 license versus the old version (the 2015 version, there’s a 2016 version that didn’t go through OSI) with the (somewhat unwieldy) SPDX identifier of https://spdx.org/licenses/Unicode-DFS-2015.html

Thanks for the update @McCoySmith ! 

So, has the OSI accepted this already or is it still under review?  If the latter, we usually wait until it's been accepted there and then add it here (OSI acceptance = automatic inclusion on SPDX License List)

As for id - seems like `Unicode-3.0` would make sense as this one actually has a version number (thank you!) - the lack of versioning in the past is what resulted in the unwieldy ids previously :)

Still awaiting OSI approval.
Maybe just hold off on SPDX until that happens?
Unicode-3.0 would work although license doesn’t use the decimal

The problem with SPDX holding off is that Fedora (and downstream derivatives of Fedora using SPDX identifiers) will likely need an SPDX identifier far in advance of OSI making its decision. Of course Fedora could use a `LicenseRef-` and later replace it with whatever identifier SPDX ends up adopting. But is there really a problem with SPDX making a decision in advance of the OSI? It seems `Unicode-3.0` is foreseeably what SPDX would end up using, even in the event that OSI never approves the license. The only possible problem would be OSI insisting on some changes to the license text and Unicode using the same version number for the revised version.
(Just noting this is _somewhat_ similar to [Unicode-DFS-2016](https://spdx.org/licenses/Unicode-DFS-2016.html), but presumably SPDX would consider this to be a different separate license.)

Indeed this is pretty close to `Unicode-DFS-2016` such that SPDX could probably deal with it by revising the markup of the latter, but I guess since it's been submitted for OSI approval it's being handled as a special case?

good catch @juhp and @richardfontana - the only differences b/w this v3 and `Unicode-DFS-2016` are the presence of the name Unicode in a couple places and the defined terms repeated in the top section - in any case, these are not substantive differences as far as SPDX matching guidelines (which it would be really nice if the OSI adopted, as I have previously suggested to the OSI boar :))

Given this, we'd use the same id `Unicode-DFS-20161 and add markup to the existing license and add that it's been OSI-approved.

While I realize this id may not be "desirable" - it was the only way we had to differentiate the license at the time it was submitted to SPDX (which was version 2.6 of the SPDX License List)

While it seems as though Unicode is making minor updates to the license to make it more re-usable - that's great, but it doesn't change the existence of `Unicode-DFS-2016` as far as I can tell.

Of course, if during the OSI process, the text is changed to be substantially different than `Unicode-DFS-2016`, then that would be a different consideration.

(note, we have an open issue as to some other slight variations at #1853 )

tagging @pchestek @webmink and @smaffulli for awareness
see and

as per our https://spdx.github.io/spdx-spec/v2.3/license-matching-guidelines-and-templates/ - the inclusion of `("SOFTWARE")` in the Notice section and instances of `the Unicode` and `Unicode` in the grant section could be considered optional

and `UNICODE INC'S DATA FILES ("DATA FILES")` would be marked as replaceable with `DATA FILES` in the Notice section

Thanks @jlovejoy and @richardfontana 

Yea I agree - personally I would prefer to see the tag `Unicode-DFS-2016` deprecated in favor of `Unicode-3`,
but that is probably a consideration after OSI approval. Conversely perhaps `Unicode-DFS-2016` could be used
in the meantime for this? (We are actually doing that currently for the Fedora unicode-ucd package.)

One possibly substantive difference (accounting for the omitable and replacable text designations on Unicode-DFS-2016) is the placement of the “COPYRIGHT AND PERMISSON NOTICE” in v3 is at the top of the license rather than underneath the  Notice to User. This effects a slight substantive change as to what must be reproduced with copies or documentation.

Also, Unicode-DFS-2016 in SPDX still shows a few instances of the word “Unicode” in the text of the license that not in red, thus indicating that it is not replaceable text. I’m assuming perhaps that was an oversight in entry of the license into SPDX? Otherwise, Unicode-DFS-2016 license is only useable by Unicode for Unicode software and data (since the definition of Data Files and Software is “Unicode Inc.’s”). Taking that out was also a substantive change relative to the OSI version of 2015.

 

FWIW, I think Unicode would prefer not to have this new license not be called just an insubstantial variant of Unicode-DFS-2016, but to get a new designation for it. TBH, it seems like the case for insubstantial variation is much better between Unicode-DFS-2015 & Unicode-DFS-2016 since there is but a single line of text (“See Terms of Use for definitions of Unicode Inc.'s Data Files and Software.”) added to 2016; otherwise 2016 & 2015 are, as far as I can tell, identical.

Re: the difference b/w `Unicode-DFS-2015` and `Unicode-DFS-2016` - the former has an obligation to provide notification in modified files in section (c), which is not present in `Unicode-DFS-2016` - so that is a substantive difference in terms of legal obligations.

There is currently no "replaceable" markup on the Unicode name in `Unicode-DFS-2016` because we generally don't add such markup unless or until we find an actual need and example of such use. We would add it now.

I'm not sure moving "COPYRIGHT AND PERMISSION NOTICE" to a difference location is substantive, as that is like a heading, but I'd want to hear other SPDX-legal thoughts on that.

Do remember: we try to not deprecate or change SPDX license ids unless it is imperative. I'm not sure "would prefer a different id" is imperative. Having two licenses listed with different ids that are the same text (as per SPDX matching guidelines) has happened, I believe one such example was due to some early OSI-approval of two license with different names but had the same text in the early days of "vanity" licenses. But I'd think no one wants to repeat that now :)

Interesting. 

So the Unicode-DFS-2015 text that SPDX has includes a section (c), but the currently-OSI-approved license doesn’t have that section https://opensource.org/license/unicode-inc-license-agreement-data-files-and-software/ (nor does it have the “See Terms of Use for definitions of Unicode Inc.'s Data Files and Software” of Unicode-DFS-2016). OSI does identify its approved version as Unicode-DFS-2015 under SPDX which seems like it’s inaccurate given the discrepancy (which I hope we’d agree is substantive). I suspect there was a version that existed before submission to OSI that had section (c), that’s the one that got the SPDX identifier, and then it was revised to remove (c) and submitted to OSI, and OSI just assumed the Unicode-DFS-2015 identifier corresponded to the version they approved.

Anyway, a bit of a mess. Probably ought to do some cleanup on it, maybe after deciding on a tag for the new license.

Thanks @McCoySmith - I also realized that this new text was raised back in Feb in #1851 (which I just closed since we have this issue going). 

Using the Wayback machine, it appears that at the URL https://www.unicode.org/license.txt :
- as of Feb 16, 2023 - the text was still a match to `Unicode-DFS-2016` up until Sept 11, 2023 when it shows the text changed to the OSI submission and version number added. This is a bit odd as the Feb issue here talks about how the license text had changed at that url back then.  
- I also realized I had reached out to Unicode based on some minor variations of `Unicode-DFS-2016` found "in the wild' - such variations were about the inclusion or omission of the NOTICE paragraph which made us/SPDX wonder if we ought to mark that as optional. - In any case, it's helpful that the current text at that same URL is now versioned, something I hope Unicode continues to do. It's also be great if any subsequent versions don't use the same URL :)

As to adding this now or waiting for the OSI to officially approve, I may just make the PR but hold off on merging it until that point.

One small request from Unicode:
They’d prefer the identifier to be Unicode-3 rather than Unicode-3.0, as they don’t do dot releases on their licenses (and this is the first one they’ve versioned, since not versioning might be part of the reason for the confusion amongst the various variations of the license).

There is some precedence for not doing dot releases on SPDX identifiers (see the BSD variants), so I’m assuming you don’t have to use decimals?

BSD-3-clause is descriptive of the # of clauses, not the license version.

However the [files](https://github.com/jtauber/pyuca/tree/v1.2/pyuca) this license applies to have different headers. The most recently added files (`allkeys-9.0.0.txt` and `allkeys-10.0.0.txt`) have a header of the form:

```

```

The mentioned URL redirects to https://www.unicode.org/copyright.html, which mentions [Unicode Data Files and Software License](https://www.unicode.org/license.txt), which is the license text under review here.

The dates differ per file. However, since they all refer to the same URL, I assume the same, most recent version of the license applies.
